Neonatal Night sharks (Carcharhinus signatus) are born at a total length of 60 cm [Lb = 60 cm], a size that is relatively modest compared to some other large carcharhinids but which reflects the constraints of a placental viviparous reproductive mode. Gestation proceeds within the uterine environment where the developing intrauterine embryo relies on a yolk-sac placenta for nutrient transfer, a strategy that allows for substantial embryonic growth before parturition. The timing of parturition is closely linked to thermal conditions, as the entire gestational period unfolds at a water temperature of 21.7 °C [T = 21.7 °C]; under these conditions, the gestation period, which is synonymous with the age at birth, has been estimated at 305 days [ab = 305 days]. This relatively protracted gestation is consistent with the life history of other slow-growing, late-maturing elasmobranchs. Following a live birth, the neonatal pups undergo a rapid transition to first exogenous feeding as they disperse into nursery grounds, where small teleost prey and cephalopods are abundant. The size at birth appears to be a critical determinant of early survival, as larger neonates are presumably better able to evade predators and capture prey during their vulnerable first weeks of life.

Females of this species ultimately reach a considerable asymptotic body size, attaining an ultimate total length of 280 cm [Li = 280 cm]. This substantial maximum length places Carcharhinus signatus among the larger members of its genus, and it is accompanied by a correspondingly high ultimate wet weight of 154,000 grams [Wwi = 154,000 grams] for adult females. This maximum body mass is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory that spans many years. The onset of reproductive capability occurs well before this asymptotic size is reached, however. In females, the onset of gonadal maturation, specifically puberty, is documented at a total length of 202 cm [Lp = 202 cm]. This size at maturity represents a point at which females have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the energetic demands of gestation and parturition. The length at which males become reproductively viable is somewhat smaller, with puberty recorded at a total length of 185 cm [Lp = 185 cm]. This sexual dimorphism in size at maturity is a common pattern among viviparous sharks and likely reflects the differential energetic costs of reproduction between the sexes.

Reproductive output in this species, observed under the prevailing thermal regime of 21.7 °C [T = 21.7 °C], is characterized by a single annual reproductive cycle. Females produce one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], a frequency that is typical for large, slow-reproducing carcharhinids. Within each annual reproductive event, litter sizes range from 4 to 12 pups [N_R_i = litter sizes range from 4 to 12 pups]. This combination of moderate fecundity and a single, well-spaced annual reproductive event is consistent with a K-selected life history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity. The total annual reproductive rate, implied by this single annual litter of 4 to 12 pups, is relatively low compared to more fecund shark species that produce larger litters or multiple litters per year. This conservative reproductive strategy makes the population particularly vulnerable to fishing pressure, as the removal of even a modest number of mature adults can have a disproportionately large impact on recruitment.

Maximum longevity for the Night shark has been estimated by analyzing growth bands in vertebral centra, with the assumption that the oldest back-calculated ages closely approximate the true lifespan of the species. Under the thermal conditions prevalent in its habitat, which average 21.7 °C [T = 21.7 °C], the lifespan is estimated at approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years]. This is a moderate lifespan for a shark of its size; some larger carcharhinids, such as the bull shark, can live considerably longer, while smaller, more fast-growing species may have shorter lifespans. The age-based demographic data indicate that individuals require several years to reach reproductive maturity, and after achieving maturity, they may experience only a limited number of breeding seasons before senescence. This life history structure, characterized by a moderate lifespan and delayed reproduction, renders the species highly susceptible to overexploitation, as it has limited capacity for rapid population recovery following significant adult mortality.

In addition to its demographic parameters, the Night shark exhibits distinct physiological and ecological traits that are characteristic of a deepwater, semi-oceanic existence. The species is commonly associated with the outer continental shelf and upper slope, where it preys primarily on mesopelagic fishes, squids, and crustaceans. Its streamlined body and moderately large pectoral fins suggest an active, cruising predatory lifestyle capable of sustained swimming over large distances. Comparative studies indicate that the body size at maturity and the relatively low fecundity are broadly similar to those of other members of the genus Carcharhinus that occupy analogous thermal and depth niches. Growth rates appear to be relatively slow, and the species likely exhibits a high degree of site fidelity to specific upwelling zones where prey is concentrated. These ecological and behavioral attributes, combined with the life history parameters described, underscore the importance of a precautionary approach to the management of this species throughout its range in the western Atlantic Ocean.
